verses.text: You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things.
And we know that God's judgment against those who do such things is based on truth.
So when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God's judgment?
Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads you to repentance?
But because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment will be revealed.
God "will repay each one according to his deeds."
To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life.
But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger.
There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek;
but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.
For God does not show favoritism.
All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.
Indeed, when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law.
So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them
on the day when God will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.
Now you, if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God;
if you know His will and approve of what is superior because you are instructed by the law;
if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?
You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?
As it is written: "God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
Circumcision has value if you observe the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
The one who is physically uncircumcised yet keeps the law will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.
A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical.
No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man's praise does not come from men, but from God.

context.author: Paul the apostle, writing through a secretary named Tertius (1:1; 16:22)
context.genre: Letter (epistle), written as a carefully argued case for the gospel
context.audience: The Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles
context.mapLabel: ROME, A MIXED CHURCH OF JEWS AND GENTILES
context.setting: Paul turns to someone who condemns the people described in chapter 1. He is probably speaking to a moral, religious person, and soon addresses a Jew by name (v.17). He argues that God judges everyone by the same standard, with no exceptions for those who have the law or the right heritage.
context.custom: Jews were proud of having the law, circumcision, and being “a guide to the blind” (vv.17-20). Paul answers by saying that what counts is a changed heart. He ends with a play on words: a true Jew is one “inwardly,” and his praise is from God, not people (vv.28-29).
context.timelineImmediate: Paul’s argument tightens in chapter 3: if everyone is guilty, what advantage does the Jew have? Then he gives the verdict in 3:9-20.
context.timelineBible: “God will repay each person according to what he has done” (v.6) quotes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12. The idea of the law written on the heart (v.15) recalls Jeremiah 31:33. Verse 24 quotes Isaiah 52:5.
context.sparkNotes: Paul says anyone who judges others is doing the same things himself, and that God judges fairly with no favorites. Those without the law have a conscience, while Jews who boast in the law but break it dishonor God. Real circumcision is a matter of the heart.

translation.meaning: Literally “receiving a face,” meaning showing favoritism. A judge who did that was corrupt. Paul says God never does.
God’s goodness. Paul says it is meant to lead to repentance, not to be taken as permission to ignore him.

otBackground.note: God repays everyone for what they have done.
God’s law written on hearts under the new covenant.
God’s name is dishonored among the nations because of his people.

overview.summary: Paul says that moral people who condemn others are guilty too, and that God will judge Jew and Gentile impartially, by the heart and not by heritage.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Corinth to the Christians in Rome.

history.t: Several synagogues existed in Rome, and Jews held a respected place, but they were often resented for their customs.
Roman Stoics also taught that people should do what they judge in others. Paul uses that common ground.

customs.t: The sign of the covenant for Jewish males. Some thought it guaranteed God’s favor, and Paul says it means nothing without obedience.
Jews were to bind the law to their hands and foreheads. Paul says the real place for it is the heart.

archaeology.t: Greek inscriptions from Jewish catacombs in Rome show a large Greek-speaking Jewish community.
Scrolls like those found at Qumran show how a Jew “rested in the law” by studying it.

overview.discussion: Paul says that judging others is easy because we excuse ourselves. Where do I most easily see someone else’s fault but miss my own?
overview.book: The letter to the Romans · 16 chapters. Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel, written to a church he had not yet visited.
overview.author: Paul
